notes: Source of truth for how reviews are rated. Edit this file to change evidence types, caps, checklists, score anchors or citations, then run `npm run docs` to regenerate docs/METHODS.md and bump `version`. Changing `version` makes every paper get a fresh review the next time it is uploaded. Caps are on a 0-5 scale in steps of 0.5.

claim_types.label: Cause or treatment effect
claim_types.description: Says X causes, prevents or treats Y in people (for example 'yoga poses reverse scoliosis').

claim_types.label: Link or association
claim_types.description: Says X is linked to Y, without claiming one causes the other (for example 'a variant is associated with higher risk').

claim_types.label: How something works
claim_types.description: Explains a biological mechanism, usually in cells, animals or another model system.

claim_types.label: Test or prediction
claim_types.description: Says a test, score or model can detect or predict an outcome.

claim_types.label: Description
claim_types.description: Reports how common something is, or what was observed, without explaining why.

evidence_types.label: Meta-analysis of randomized trials
evidence_types.examples: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses that pool randomized trials.
checklist: Was the question and protocol registered in advance?
Was the literature search thorough, and were unpublished studies sought?
Did the authors assess risk of bias in each included trial, and account for it?
Were the pooled studies similar enough to combine (heterogeneity)?
Was publication bias assessed?

evidence_types.label: Randomized trial
evidence_types.examples: Participants assigned to groups by chance.
checklist: Was assignment truly random and concealed until enrollment?
Were participants, carers and outcome assessors blinded where possible?
How many dropped out, and were all randomized participants analysed?
Was the primary outcome pre-registered and reported as planned?
Is the sample large enough for the effect claimed?
evidence_types.cap_note: A single trial is capped below 5 because one trial, however good, still needs replication.

evidence_types.label: Observational study with a causal design
evidence_types.examples: Mendelian randomization, natural experiments, target trial emulation.
checklist: Are the design's key assumptions stated and tested (for example instrument validity in Mendelian randomization)?
Is the comparison clearly defined, with a clear start of follow-up?
Were sensitivity analyses run for the main assumptions?
Could the result be explained by selection into the study or loss to follow-up?

evidence_types.label: Observational study
evidence_types.examples: Cohort, case-control, cross-sectional and biobank or health-record studies.
checklist: Were the groups comparable at the start, and how were they selected?
Were important other explanations (confounders) measured and adjusted for?
Were exposure and outcome measured the same way in every group?
How complete was follow-up?
Do the authors use causal language the design can't support?
evidence_types.cap_note: Causal claims are capped at 3 because people choose their own exposures, so other differences between groups can explain the result.

evidence_types.label: Genetic association study
evidence_types.examples: GWAS, exome-wide association, rare-variant burden tests, family-based association.
checklist: Was the significance threshold corrected for the number of tests (for example genome-wide significance)?
Was the finding replicated in an independent sample?
Was population structure or relatedness controlled?
Which ancestries were studied, and does the claim generalize beyond them?
For rare variants: how were variants called, filtered and classified?
evidence_types.cap_note: Association claims can be strong with replication. Causal or clinical claims are capped at 2 because an associated variant is not necessarily the causal one, and associations don't establish clinical usefulness.

evidence_types.label: Diagnostic or prediction model study
evidence_types.examples: Test accuracy studies, risk scores, clinical prediction and machine-learning models.
checklist: Were participants representative of the people the test is meant for?
Was the reference standard applied to everyone, blind to the test result?
Was the model validated on data it was not built from, ideally from another setting?
Are accuracy, calibration and the number of events reported?
evidence_types.cap_note: Diagnostic claims are capped at 4; reserve 4 for models validated independently in a different setting.

evidence_types.label: Laboratory or animal study
checklist: Were animals or samples randomized to groups, and were assessors blinded?
Was the sample size justified, and were experiments independently repeated?
Were appropriate controls used?
Are all outcomes and excluded animals or samples reported?
How far is the model from the human condition the paper talks about?
evidence_types.cap_note: Mechanistic claims about the model system can score up to 4. Claims about human treatment are capped at 2 because most findings in animals and cells don't carry over to people.

evidence_types.label: Case report or case series
evidence_types.examples: Descriptions of one patient or a group of patients without a comparison group.
checklist: Were cases included consecutively, with clear criteria?
Is the condition and its measurement described in enough detail?
Is follow-up complete and long enough?
Are alternative explanations for the outcome discussed?
evidence_types.cap_note: Without a comparison group, a case series can't show that a treatment caused an outcome.

evidence_types.label: Narrative review or commentary
evidence_types.examples: Reviews without a systematic search, opinion pieces, perspectives.
checklist: Are the claims supported by cited primary studies?
Does the review present evidence on both sides?
Does it distinguish strong evidence from weak?
evidence_types.effect_label: How well the claims are backed
evidence_types.cap_note: A review that isn't systematic can't be stronger than the evidence it chooses to cite.

evidence_types.label: Other design
evidence_types.examples: Qualitative research, methods papers, simulations, or designs that don't fit above.
checklist: Is the method appropriate for the question?
Is it compared against existing approaches or a reasonable baseline?
Could someone else reproduce it from what is reported?

rigor.label: Study quality
rigor.definition: How well the study was carried out, judged against the best possible version of its own design (use the checklist for its evidence type). A well-run observational study can score high here even though its causal claims are capped.

anchors.5: No meaningful flaws for this design.
anchors.4: Minor flaws, unlikely to change the conclusion.
anchors.3: Flaws that could change the size of the effect, but probably not its direction.
anchors.2: Serious flaws that could explain the result on their own.
anchors.1: Flaws so severe the result can't be interpreted.
anchors.0: Not a real test of the question.

bias.label: Risk of slanted reporting
bias.definition: Risks that study quality doesn't cover: conflicts of interest and funding, selective reporting of outcomes or analyses, and spin (conclusions, abstract or title that go beyond the results).

anchors.0: Independent authors, outcomes reported as planned, conclusions match the results.
anchors.1: Minor issues, such as a declared conflict with no sign it shaped the reporting.
anchors.2: Some spin or a relevant conflict, but the main results are reported fairly.
anchors.3: Clear spin, or outcomes that seem selectively reported, or an undeclared relevant conflict.
anchors.4: Several of the above, and they push in the direction the authors favour.
anchors.5: Reporting is so slanted that the paper can't be taken at face value.

effect.label: Evidence for the main claim
effect.definition: How strongly the paper supports its own main claim. First identify the main claim and its type. The score can't exceed the cap for this evidence type and claim type, and is lowered further for flaws, imprecision, or results that conflict with other research.

anchors.5: Strong, consistent evidence that would be hard to overturn.
anchors.4: Good evidence; further research is unlikely to reverse it.
anchors.3: Moderate evidence; the claim is plausible but could change.
anchors.2: Weak evidence; consistent with the claim but other explanations remain likely.
anchors.1: Very weak evidence; the data barely bear on the claim.
anchors.0: No evidence for the claim, or the data point the other way.

value.label: Usefulness
value.definition: What the paper is good for: changing practice, informing decisions alongside other evidence, or pointing to what should be tested next.

anchors.5: Practice-changing; requires strong, replicated evidence in the people it applies to.
anchors.4: Should inform decisions alongside other evidence.
anchors.3: Adds meaningfully to the evidence on its question.
anchors.2: Worth testing further; a reason to run a better study.
